In this manuscript, Pasca et al. conduct an analysis of the UK Biobank to examine the relationship between mitochondrial
DNA (mtDNA) heteroplasmy and the risk of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). Their study demonstrates that deleterious
mitochondrial heteroplasmy associates with increased incident risk of CLL and may serve as a novel predictor of CLL risk,
highlighting a promising new biomarker for CLL.
The authors have adequately addressed the prior comments from Reviewers 1 and 3. However, several important issues
remain, and the following comments will help improve the clarity of the manuscript.
Here is my additional major concern on this Manuscript:
• It is unclear why the 5% VAF threshold was set for mitochondrial heteroplasmy. Lower-frequency variants may reflect lower
level heteroplasmy that is still important biologically. By using a 5% VAF cutoff, you may be missing some of these very early
clonal events that are biologically important. Many recent mtDNA studies now use methods that can detect variants below
1% (https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0000000000200745). If the reason for using the 5% threshold was to limit
analysis to larger clones, then it would be helpful to know whether patients with heteroplasmy and VAF <5% have similar or
abrogated clinical associations.
• Variant filtering included mtDNA-CN thresholds, but mtDNA-CN is itself a strong marker of hematopoietic aging and may
be associated with CH and leukemia risk. Because both heteroplasmy detection and mMSS may be influenced by mtDNA-
CN, failing to control for mtDNA-CN in the regression models may confound the observed associations. Please provide
models adjusted for mtDNA-CN and test for interaction between mtDNA-CN and heteroplasmy/mMSS. It would be helpful to
know whether mtDNA-CN differs between L-CHIP positive and negative individuals.
• The authors state that many heteroplasmies are somatic, but this is assumed rather than demonstrated. Because the
prevalence of germline mtDNA heteroplasmy varies substantially across mitochondrial haplogroups, ancestry groups, and
maternal age, the current analyses may be confounded by background population structure. The authors should provide a
sensitivity analysis excluding common germline heteroplasmies.

marker of clonal expansion that occurs with age” — cite recent single-cell mtDNA studies to strengthen these statements

## Paper

## Abstract

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) can arise from lymphoid clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (L-CHIP), but many individuals who develop CLL lack detectable L-CHIP prior to diagnosis. To identify additional predictors of CLL risk, we analyze mitochondrial heteroplasmy in 419,154 individuals from the UK Biobank (UKB). Heteroplasmy is associated with a 1.5-fold increased risk of developing CLL, and this risk rises to 4-fold when accounting for deleterious heteroplasmic variants. These findings are confirmed in an independent cohort, the All of Us Research Program (AoU). Notably, the associations remain significant even in the absence of L-CHIP, highlighting heteroplasmy’s potential utility as an independent biomarker. Moreover, heteroplasmy is enriched in individuals with high-risk L-CHIP genotypes and large clonal burden, suggesting a potential biological role in malignant transformation. Here, we show that mitochondrial heteroplasmy, especially functionally deleterious variants, identifies individuals at increased risk of CLL who would otherwise go undetected by L-CHIP-based assessments.

---

## Introduction

With ageing, stem cells acquire an increasing number of somatic DNA alterations, including mutations and chromosomal aberration (CA). These DNA defects mark a genetically distinct cell population, a condition also known as somatic mosaicism. Occasionally, somatic DNA changes confer functional consequences leading to a relative growth advantage of the mutated cell 1–4. In the context of hematopoiesis, such clonal expansion of a hematopoietic stem cell is known as clonal hematopoiesis (CH) 5–7. Many leukemia-associated genes and mosaic CAs have been found in individuals with CH and have been associated with increased risk of hematologic malignancies 4,6–8. A distinct classification of CH has been proposed based on the association between various genotypes and hematologic malignancy 8. Myeloid clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (M-CHIP), defined as the expansion of a hematopoietic clone(s) carrying somatic mutation(s) found in myeloid neoplasms (MN) 9,10, is the most frequent. A subset of CH with somatic mutations observed in lymphoid malignancies represents lymphoid CHIP (L-CHIP) 8. Even though L-CHIP is associated with the incidence of lymphoid malignancies, mainly chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), many individuals who develop CLL do not have L-CHIP present years prior to clinical diagnosis 8. Thus, L-CHIP only captures a subset of individuals who will develop CLL.

Because mitochondria have a less efficient DNA repair system compared to the nucleus, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is more prone to mutations 11,12. Heteroplasmy is defined as the presence of these mutations in only a subset of mtDNA. Given the frequent occurrence of mtDNA mutations, heteroplasmy has been commonly used as a clonal marker 13. We have shown that heteroplasmy occurring in the hematopoietic system is associated with incident hematologic malignancy in general 14. In addition, we have demonstrated that likely deleterious heteroplasmies are associated with incident MN 15, suggesting that heteroplasmy is not only a clonal marker, but may play a biological role in the development of hematologic malignancies.

Here, we show that heteroplasmy is an independent predictor of CLL in general and in conjunction with L-CHIP.

---

## Results

Cohort characteristics
The study included 419,154 individuals from the UKB with available whole exome sequencing (WES) and whole genome sequencing (WGS) data. Individuals with prevalent CLL or unexplained lymphocytosis (absolute lymphocyte count over 5000/µL) were excluded from the analysis. The median (Q1, Q3) [range] age was 58 (50, 63) [38, 72] years, 45.8% (n=191,926) were men, and 94.4% (n=395,819) were self-identified as White.

Using WES data restricted to 235 genes involved in lymphoid malignancies (Supplementary Table 1) 8, we identified a total of 12,683 L-CHIP mutations at a variant allele fraction (VAF) ≥ 2%, which were present in 10,746 (2.6%) individuals, similarly low to the previously published 1.3% (Supplementary Table 2) 8. The L-CHIP mutations were evenly distributed among various genes, without the distinct predominance that is typically observed in M-CHIP (Fig. 1A). Similarly to previous reports, DUSP22, FAT1, KMT2D, SYNE1, ATM, KMT2C, PCLO, SPEN, ARID1A, NEB, MGA, RP1L1, SMARCA4, CIITA, DLC1, PTPRD, ATR were most commonly mutated L-CHIP genes 8. Most individuals with L-CHIP had only one mutation, with multiple mutations seen in only 11.5% of those with L-CHIP (n=1232) (Fig. 1B). L-CHIP was significantly associated with older age (P<0.0001) and smoking status (P<0.01) (Table 1 and Fig. 1C). These associations were attenuated but remained significant when comparing individuals with L-CHIP only to those without either L-CHIP or M-CHIP (Table 2).

MtDNA heteroplasmy was identified from WGS data using the MitoHPC pipeline at a VAF threshold of 5% (VAF 5-95%) as previously described 16. Because of this threshold, the observed heteroplasmies likely represented mutations that underwent clonal expansion, rather than the full underlying mtDNA mutational rate, as very small clones would not be detected. For each mtDNA variant, we used a modified mitochondrial DNA local constraint (mMLC) score, which quantifies the local tolerance to base or amino acid substitution for each base pair in the mtDNA genome and thus predicts the likely deleterious effects of each variant 17. To capture the overall impact of multiple heteroplasmies in a given individual, we generated the mMLC score sum (mMSS) by adding all mMLC scores for that individual. Heteroplasmy was present in 118,493 (28.3%) individuals, with Complex I and D-loop as the most frequently mutated complexes/regions (Supplementary Fig. 1A). We observed differences in mMSS across complexes/regions, with the D-loop presenting some of the lowest mMSS values, while tRNA and rRNA presented some of the highest mMSS values (Supplementary Fig. 1B). Among those with heteroplasmy, 22,720 (19.2%) had multiple heteroplasmies (Supplementary Fig. 1C). With regards to phenotype associations, we observed that heteroplasmy was more frequent in older individuals and in smokers (Supplementary Table 3).

Further, we analyzed a random subset of the All of Us Research Program (AoU, n=40,930) to confirm our findings in an independent cohort. Heteroplasmy was present in 11,064 (27.0%) individuals with a distribution of heteroplasmy count and mMSS similar to that observed in the UKB (Supplementary Fig. 2A). More specifically, Complex I and D-loop were the most frequently mutated complex/region. In addition, D-loop and the highest in tRNA and rRNA presented some of the lowest mMSS values (Supplementary Fig. 2B), consistent with the findings in the UKB.

Among those with heteroplasmy, 2086 (18.9%) had multiple heteroplasmies (Supplementary Fig. 2C). Individuals who were older or ever smokers were also more likely to have heteroplasmy (Supplementary Table 4).

Heteroplasmy and the risk of CLL
We have previously reported an association between heteroplasmy and incident hematologic malignancies, particularly MN 14,15. Here, we sought to determine whether the presence of heteroplasmy in the general population was associated with an increased risk of CLL. The incidence of CLL in the UKB was 0.1% (463 cases) with a median follow-up of 13.8 (13.0, 14.5) years. Compared to those without heteroplasmy, individuals with 1 or more heteroplasmies had a higher risk of developing CLL even after adjusting for age, sex, smoking status, and a history of cancer (hazard ratio [HR]=1.5; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.3–1.8; P<0.0001) (Fig. 2A). All subsequent analyses in this paper included age, sex, smoking status, and a history of cancer as covariates.

Both heteroplasmy count (HR=1.4; 95% CI 1.2–1.5; P<0.0001) and mMSS (HR=4.2; 95% CI 3.2–5.5; P<0.0001) were associated with a higher risk of incident CLL. In addition, when including heteroplasmy count and mMSS in the same model, heteroplasmy count (HR=1.0; 95% CI 0.9–1.2; P=0.76) was not associated with CLL incidence, while mMSS (HR=4.0; 95% CI 2.7–5.9; P<0.0001) remained a significant risk factor for CLL (Fig. 2B). Since higher mMSS indicates the presence of likely deleterious variants, its significant association with CLL incidence, after adjusting for heteroplasmy count, suggests possible causal effect rather than merely a marker of clonal expansion.

Next, we sought to determine if the location of mtDNA mutations had a differential effect on the development of CLL vs. MN. We observed that higher mMSS in complex IV was more strongly associated with MN than CLL (Supplementary Table 5 and Supplementary Fig. 3).

To test the robustness of the heteroplasmy VAF filter used, we reevaluated the association between heteroplasmy count/mMSS and CLL incidence using heteroplasmy at 3% and 10% VAF (Supplementary Table 6). We observed that results remained consistent even when using different VAF thresholds.

Given the role of mtDNA-CN as a marker of hematopoietic aging and the interplay between mtDNA-CN and blood counts, we also evaluated the association between heteroplasmy count/mMSS and CLL incidence when adjusting for mtDNA-CN and for blood counts (absolute neutrophil count, absolute lymphocyte count, absolute monocyte count, red blood cell count and platelet count) (Supplementary Table 7). Even after adjusting for mtDNA-CN and blood counts, heteroplasmy count and mMSS remained associated with CLL incidence.

We observed similar associations between heteroplasmy and CLL in an independent cohort, the AoU, using a case-cohort design. In addition to the random subset of 20% of the eligible participants (n=40,930), we identified all other cases of CLL in AoU (n=56), leading to a total of 87 CLL cases in the case-cohort, with a median follow-up of 3.9 (1.6–4.6) years. After adjusting for age, sex, and smoking status, individuals with ≥1 heteroplasmies had a higher risk of developing CLL compared to those without heteroplasmy (HR 2.0; 95% CI 1.3–3.1; P=0.001) (Supplementary Fig. 4A). Both heteroplasmy count (HR 1.5; 95% CI 1.2–1.8; P=0.001) and mMSS (HR 4.1; 95% CI 2.5–6.8; P<0.0001) were associated with an increased risk of CLL. In addition, when both heteroplasmy and mMSS were included in the same model, mMSS (HR 4.3; 95% CI 1.9–9.4; P<0.001) remained significantly associated with CLL incidence while heteroplasmy count was not (HR 1.0; 95% CI 0.7–1.4; P=0.89) (Supplementary Fig. 4B).

The effect of L-CHIP on CLL incidence
Consistent with previous findings 8, we observed that L-CHIP was associated with incident CLL (HR=5.1; 95% CI 3.9–6.7; P<0.0001) (Fig. 3A). Next, we sought to determine if clonal burden (maximum VAF per individual) and number of mutations were also associated with incident CLL. We observed that, relative to individuals without L-CHIP, both VAF≥10% (HR=6.9; 95% CI 4.9–9.6; P<0.0001) and multiple mutations (HR=12.7; 95% CI 7.7–21.0; P<0.0001) were associated with a higher risk of incident CLL (Fig. 3A).

We then evaluated the association between the recurrent L-CHIP gene mutations and the incidence of CLL. We identified eight high-risk genes: MYD88, IGLL5, NOTCH1, XPO1, LTB, TCL1A, TAF1 and DUSP2 (Fig. 3B and Supplementary Table 8). In contrast, M-CHIP was not associated with CLL incidence in L-CHIP negative individuals (HR=1.3; 95% CI 0.9–1.8; P=0.11).

Association between L-CHIP and heteroplasmy
We and others 14,18–20 observed that a notable number of heteroplasmies are somatic, and thus, mark the clonal expansion of the cells in which they occur. Using WGS, somatic heteroplasmy can only be detected when the mutation-carrying clone is significantly expanded relative to polyclonal counterparts. Previously, we have shown that likely functional heteroplasmy was associated with the presence of M-CHIP 15. Thus, we expected to find a similar association between heteroplasmy and L-CHIP. L-CHIP and heteroplasmy were concurrently present in 0.8% of individuals, while 27.5% and 1.8% of individuals were found to have either heteroplasmy or L-CHIP only, respectively (Fig. 4A). Notably, heteroplasmy was more common in L-CHIP carriers compared to individuals without L-CHIP (31.4% vs 28.2%; P<0.0001) (Fig. 4B). Among L-CHIP carriers, heteroplasmy was significantly associated with large L-CHIP clones (VAF≥10%) (33.4% vs 29.6%; P<0.001) but not with multiple mutations (33.0% vs 31.2%; P=0.14) (Fig. 4B). Heteroplasmy was also significantly more common in individuals with high-risk L-CHIP genotypes (39.0% vs 31.1%; P<0.01) (Fig. 4B and Supplementary Fig. 5). Among individuals with heteroplasmy, those with L-CHIP were more likely to have multiple heteroplasmies compared to those without L-CHIP (21.9% vs 19.1%; P<0.001) (Fig. 4C). Only L-CHIP clonal burden (VAF≥10%) (23.9% vs 20.0%; P=0.01), but not multiple L-CHIP mutations (21.2% vs 22.0%; P=0.80) nor high-risk L-CHIP mutations (23.0% vs 21.9%; P=0.99), was associated with the presence of multiple heteroplasmies (Fig. 4C).

To determine whether the higher prevalence of heteroplasmy in L-CHIP was just a marker of CH (passenger mtDNA mutations) rather than having a functional impact, we assessed the association between L-CHIP and mMSS. Because mMSS comprises not only the functional prediction of each variant but also the sum of all heteroplasmies in an individual, our analysis was adjusted for heteroplasmy count. Among those with heteroplasmy, mMSS was significantly higher in L-CHIP, particularly in individuals with higher clonal burden (VAF≥10%) and with multiple L-CHIP mutations. Even though not statistically significant, there was a trend towards significance for mMSS and high-risk L-CHIP genotypes compared to other L-CHIP (Fig. 4D, Supplementary Fig. 5 and Supplementary Table 9). Overall, these data suggest that the presence of mtDNA mutations may not only be a marker of clonal expansion but may also play an important role in clonal expansion and malignant transformation.

Previously, we have shown that M-CHIP and its high-risk subtypes are associated with heteroplasmy 15. In the current study, we observed that L-CHIP was significantly associated with M-CHIP (P<0.0001). To ensure M-CHIP was not a confounder, we excluded individuals with M-CHIP mutations and found that heteroplasmy was more prevalent in L-CHIP (P<0.0001), large L-CHIP clones (VAF≥10%) (P=0.02) and high-risk L-CHIP mutations (P=0.02). Moreover, we observed that mMSS was higher in individuals with L-CHIP (P<0.0001) and those with multiple L-CHIP mutations (P=0.02) (Supplementary Table 10), indicating its possible functional effect.

The impact of concurrent L-CHIP and heteroplasmy on the risk of CLL
We then explored the potential interaction between L-CHIP and heteroplasmy on CLL risk (Fig. 5A). Both, L-CHIP (HR=5.3; 95% CI 3.7–7.5; P<0.0001) and heteroplasmy alone (HR=1.5; 95% CI 1.2–1.8; P<0.0001) were independent risk factors for CLL (Fig. 5B). The risk of CLL was over 7-fold higher in individuals with concurrent L-CHIP and heteroplasmy (Fig. 5B).

Since heteroplasmy was associated with high-risk L-CHIP, we examined whether heteroplasmy was associated with incident CLL after adjusting for L-CHIP properties (large L-CHIP clones [VAF≥10%], multiple mutations, and high-risk L-CHIP mutations). Among L-CHIP individuals, neither the presence of heteroplasmy (HR=1.2; 95% CI 0.7–2.0; P=0.54), nor mMSS (HR=1.2; 95% CI 0.5–3.2; P=0.66), analyzed in independent models, were significantly associated with an increased risk of CLL after accounting for L-CHIP properties (Fig. 5C). Although these results suggest that heteroplasmy does not provide additional prognostic value in individuals with L-CHIP, heteroplasmy may still be biologically relevant in this population.

Since the majority of UKB individuals who developed CLL did not have L-CHIP (87.3%) (Fig. 5A), we examined whether heteroplasmy was an independent risk factor for CLL in those without L-CHIP. We found that the presence of heteroplasmy was associated 1.5-fold increase in the CLL risk (HR=1.5; 95% CI 1.2–1.8; P<0.0001). In addition, mMSS was associated with CLL incidence even after adjusting for heteroplasmy count (HR=4.1; 95% CI 2.7–6.1; P<0.0001), suggesting that deleterious heteroplasmies may have a direct functional impact on CLL development (Fig. 5D).

---

## Methods

The UK Biobank (UKB) was approved by the UK Biobank Research Ethics Committee, and all participants provided written informed consent before participation. Informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in the study, and the protocol was reviewed by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the All of Us Research Program.

Study population
The UKB is a large population-based prospective study of ~500,000 individuals between the ages of 40–69 years across the United Kingdom, recruited from 2006 to 2010 32. The UKB has extensive information on individual’s genetic and phenotypic data, including demographics and lifestyle factors. The data is linked to the death registry, cancer registry, hospital admissions, and primary care visit data.

We have previously described our filtering approach 15. Briefly, from the standpoint of heteroplasmy we excluded samples that presented either of the following criteria: 1) potential mitochondrial contamination (a contamination level ≥ 3% from Haplocheck (https://github.com/genepi/haplocheck) 34); 2) 2 or more heteroplasmic variants part of different haplogroups; 3) 2 or more variant matching to the same nuclear mitochondrial sequences (NUMT); 4) low minimum base coverage (<100) or low mean base coverage (<500); 5) low mtDNA copy number (mtDNA-CN) (≤40); 6) heteroplasmy count ≥ 6. We also excluded individuals based on missing data (M-CHIP, tobacco smoking, blood counts) or that were ineligible due to a history of MN or presence of a potential myeloproliferative neoplasm 15. In addition to these criteria, we excluded individuals with missing L-CHIP data (n=14,267), those with an excess of L-CHIP variants (n=0), those with a history of CLL (n=201) and those with lymphocytosis (>5000/µL; n=682). Finally, we included a total of 419,154 individuals.

The All of Us Research Program (AoU) is a large population-based cohort study including diverse populations over the age of 18 living in the US 35. It includes physical measurements, a survey of lifestyle factors, and a biospecimen for DNA collected at enrollment, in addition to linkage to electronic health records data. For this study, 317,964 individuals with short-read whole genome sequencing and electronic health records from the Controlled Data Repository v8 (C2024Q3R4, released on February 3, 2025) were considered. From these individuals, we constructed a case-cohort—a valid and efficient study design particularly useful when exposure assessment is resource-intensive or costly 36 using individuals free of cancer, cardiovascular disease, or sepsis at the time of DNA collection (n=248,388). We have further excluded a total of 24,290 individuals for either missing smoking information (n=7172) or having DNA from samples other than blood (n=17,781). Of these participants, 61 were excluded during heteroplasmy filtering steps. We then randomly selected 20% of the individuals as the subcohort (n=40,930), including 31 individuals who developed CLL. We further identified all other cases of CLL in AoU (n=56), leading to a total of 87 CLL cases in the case-cohort.

Definition of lymphocytosis and cytopenias
Lymphocytosis was defined as an absolute lymphocyte count over 5000/µL. Anemia was defined as a hemoglobin concentration under 13 g/dL in men and under 12 g/dL in women. Thrombocytopenia was defined as a platelet count under 150,000/µL 37,38.

Heteroplasmy and mitochondrial DNA copy number analysis in the UKB
Samples for DNA were collected on the baseline visit, and DNA was extracted from buffy coat using the Maxwell® 16 Instrument (Promega) and the Maxwell® 16 Blood DNA Purification Kit (Promega–AS1010X). WGS CRAM files from the UKB were processed on the DNA Nexus server. For heteroplasmy identification, we used the MitoHPC pipeline (version 20230418; all default settings with default random downsampling to use at most 222K reads) 16, implementing GATK Mutect2 39,40. We defined a heteroplasmic SNV at a VAF of 5%, meaning that VAFs of 5–95% within an individual are defined as heteroplasmic. Alleles less than 5% or greater than 95% are classified as homoplasmic. The MitoHPC pipeline incorporates haplogrep (https://github.com/seppinho/haplogrep-cmd/v2.4.0) 41 to identify haplogroups and Haplocheck (https://github.com/genepi/haplocheck) 34 to detect in-sample contamination by detecting two different mitochondrial haplotypes in each sample. For the mtDNA-CN calculation, we used SAMtools 42 embedded in MitoHPC to generate read count and coverage information, using the command ‘samtools idxstats’. A detailed documentation on how to run MitoHPC on the DNA Nexus server is available: https://github.com/ArkingLab/MitoHPC/blob/main/docs/DNAnexus_CLOUD.md.

All 490,355 WGS samples processed using MitoHPC variant calling were successfully completed 16. The median (range) mtDNA coverage was 904x (500x-1887x).

Heteroplasmy filtering for variants
MitoHPC provides various variant annotations to evaluate variant quality, allowing us to remove low-quality variants prior to analysis. We excluded variants with read depth <300 and those flagged as base quality, mapping quality, strand bias, slippage, weak evidence, position, clustered, fragment length, and haplotype flags in the FILTER column of the VCF. We further excluded heteroplasmic variants at poly-C homopolymer regions on the mitochondrial chromosome (the list is provided as HP.bed.gz in https://github.com/dpuiu/MitoHPC). INDELs are also excluded because they are often found in homopolymer regions, where it is challenging to accurately call heteroplasmies 16.

Mitochondrial local constraint (MLC) score
The mitochondrial local constraint (MLC) score is a metric reflecting local tolerance to substitutions of base or amino acid. It is calculated for every possible mtDNA SNV by applying a sliding window method 17. To account for heteroplasmic variants that also present as homoplasmic in the population, we refined the MLC score to account for the frequency of homoplasy in the UKB population by calculating the modified MLC (mMLC) as MLC/(1+log10(number of individuals with homoplasmy in the UKB+1)). mMLC was calculated using the individuals with a given homoplasmic variant in the UKB. To capture the functional impact of multiple heteroplasmies, we calculated an mMLC score sum (mMSS) by summing all mMLC scores within a given individual.

Heteroplasmy and mitochondrial DNA copy number analysis in the AoU
In the AoU, we called mitochondrial heteroplasmy and copy number from short-read WGS data using the same pipeline and filtering steps as we did for the UKB on the All of Us Researcher Workbench. The median (range) mtDNA coverage was 1096x (576x-1288x).

CHIP variant calling
WES CRAM files were aligned to hg38. Variant calling was performed using Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) v. 4.2.2. Mutect2 39,43. Mutect2 was run in ‘tumor-only’ mode using non-default parameters: gatk Mutect2… --panel-of-normals ${ref_pon} --germline-resource ${ref_germ}. Raw variants called by Mutect2 were filtered out with FilterMutectCalls using the estimated prior probability of a reading orientation artifact generated by LearnReadOrientationModel.

L-CHIP variant filtering
Variants were annotated using ANNOVAR 44 and filtered based on a pathogenic track and a putative track adapted from a previously published paper 8 and the resulted variants were further filtered in a combined track, as described below. Variants occurring on genes located on the X chromosome in males had their VAFs divided by 2.

Pathogenic track: (1) The presence in a custom L-CHIP gene panel (Supplementary Table 1); (2) a previously published list of variants 8; (3) Mutect2 FILTER of PASS or germline; (4) depth ≥ 20; (5) alternate allele count ≥ 3 in the case of SNVs; (6) alternate allele count ≥ 5 in the case of multinucleotide variants (MNV); (7) ALTF1R2 ≥ 1; (8) ALTF2R1 ≥ 1; (9) VAF ≥ 2% in the case of SNVs; (10) VAF ≥ 10% in the case of MNVs; (11) exclusion of synonymous SNVs; (12) the maximum allele frequency across non-cancer populations (non_cancer_AF_popmax) under 0.001 in the gnomAD exome collection v2.1.1 45.

Putative track: (1) The presence in a custom L-CHIP gene panel (Supplementary Table 1); (2) Mutect2 FILTER of PASS of germline; (3) depth ≥ 20; (4) alternate allele count ≥ 5 regardless of variant type; (5) ALTF1R2 ≥ 2; (6) ALTF2R1 ≥ 2; (7) VAF ≥ 2% in the case of SNVs; (8) VAF ≥ 10% in the case of MNVs; (9) VAF ≤ 20%; (10) exclusion of synonymous SNVs; (11) the maximum allele frequency across non-cancer populations (non_cancer_AF_popmax) under 0.001 in the gnomAD exome collection v2.1.1 45.

Combined track: (1) if a variant was called by both the pathogenic and putative track, only the pathogenic track variant was kept; (2) if a variant occurred > 1% of the cohort, the variant was removed; (3) variants with VAF ≥ 35% were removed, unless they were a known pathogenic nonsynonymous variant; (4) if a gene was mutated in more than 0.05% of the cohort, non-singleton variants in that gene were assessed and were removed all variants that occurred more than the median frequency of variants in that gene as long as the removed variants occurred 10 or more times and the removed variant was not a known pathogenic variant as reported by a previously published variant list 8.

M-CHIP variant calling, and variant filtering were previously described 15. SETDB1 was removed from the M-CHIP panel because it was also present in the L-CHIP panel.

On the sample level, we excluded individuals with an excess of L-CHIP variants considered as more than 3 mutations, all of which are represented by MNVs and individuals with more than 10 CHIP variants. Large CHIP clones were defined as those having a VAF ≥ 10%. Small CHIP clones were defined as having a VAF ≥ 2% and < 10%.

High-risk L-CHIP genes mutations were assessed within individuals with L-CHIP. For a gene to be considered high-risk, it had to present the following criteria: (1) had a significant positive association with incident CLL; (2) presented an HR greater than 1 in the multivariable Cox proportional hazards model where CLL incidence was the dependent variable; (3) was present in two or more individuals that developed CLL.

Definition of CLL
In the UKB, CLL was defined using ICD-9 204.1 and ICD-10 C91.1 codes from the cancer registry linked to the UKB collected on December 22, 2022.

In The AoU CLL was defined using ICD-9 (204.1), ICD-10 (C91.1), and SNOMED (92814006).

Statistical analysis
Categorical data was represented as an absolute count (percent). Frequencies of two categorical variables were analyzed using Fisher’s exact test. Normality of the distribution was assessed using skewness, kurtosis and histogram visualization. Continuous variables were presented as median (Q1, Q3) for variables with a non-Gaussian distribution. Differences between two groups with non-Gaussian distribution were assessed using the Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon rank sum test. We used multivariable logistic regression models to evaluate the associations between CHIP and a binary variable for heteroplasmy. For the association between CHIP and mMSS, we used multivariable linear regression models. If the dependent variable was right skewed, we added 1 and log10-transformed it. The analyses were adjusted for age modeled as a restricted cubic spline (with 4 degrees of freedom), sex, tobacco smoking status (never or ever), and a history of cancer. Differences between two HR and corresponding 95% CIs were assessed using z-score=(coefficient1 - coefficient2)/(square root(standard error1^2 + standard error2^2)). The z-score was then converted to a p-value using the pnorm function in R.

For survival analysis, we used time from DNA collection to the development of CLL, death, or end of follow-up (administrative censoring on December 22, 2022), whichever occurred first. The cumulative incidence of CLL was presented as Kaplan-Meier curves. Hazard ratios and corresponding 95% confidence intervals were estimated using a multivariable Cox proportional hazards model, adjusting for age (restricted cubic splines with 4 degrees of freedom), sex, tobacco smoking (never or ever), and a history of cancer.

Robustness of the heteroplasmy VAF filter was assessed by evaluating the association between heteroplasmy count/mMSS and CLL incidence using heteroplasmy at 3%, 5% and 10% VAF cut-offs.

To assess if the association between heteroplasmy count/mMSS and CLL incidence is independent of mtDNA-CN and blood counts, we reevaluated the association between heteroplasmy count/mMSS and CLL incidence when adjusting for age, modeled as a restricted cubic spline (with 4 degrees of freedom), sex, tobacco smoking status (never or ever), a history of cancer, mtDNA-CN (natural log-transformed) and blood counts (absolute neutrophil count, absolute lymphocyte count, absolute monocyte count, red blood cell count and platelet count).

In the AoU, to account for case-cohort design, we applied appropriate weights to Cox proportional hazards models 46 to evaluate the association between mitochondrial heteroplasmy measures and incidence of CLL. As we have already excluded individuals with previous cancer, we adjusted for age (restricted cubic spline with 4 degrees of freedom), genetically determined sex, and smoking status (never or never).

We have replicated our findings in the All of Us Research Program, a large population-
based cohort study including diverse populations living in the US (All of Us Research
Program Investigators et al., 2019). From the 317,964 individuals with short-read whole
genome sequencing and electronic health records data, we implemented a case-cohort
study design, which is a cost-effective design while providing valid estimates from an
existing cohort. The case-cohort includes a subcohort (20%) of individuals randomly
selected from the eligible cohort of individuals who did not have a history of cancer and all
individuals who developed CLL. Of the 40,986 individuals included in the case-cohort
design, 87 (31 from the random sample and 56 from the remaining AoU participants
eligible for this study) developed CLL with a median (Q1, Q3) follow up of 3.9 (1.6–4.6)
years. In the random subcohort (n = 40,930), heteroplasmy was identified in 11,064
(27.0%) individuals. The distribution of heteroplasmy count (median 0; range 0 – 5) and
mMSS (median 0; range 0–2.58) were similar to those observed in the UK Biobank. After
adjusting for age (restricted cubic splines with 4 degrees of freedom), sex, and smoking
status (never vs. ever), the HR (95% CI) between mMSS and incident CLL was 4.1 (95% CI
2.5–6.8; P = 4.5x10-8), similar to what we observed in the UK Biobank. We also found an
increased risk of CLL among people with any heteroplasmy (HR 2.0; 95% CI 1.3–3.1; P =
0.001) or a higher heteroplasmy count (HR 1.5; 95% CI 1.2–1.8; P = 0.001) compared to
those who did not have heteroplasmy. As whole exome sequencing was not performed in
the All of Us Research Program to call CHIP, we performed the replication only for the
association between heteroplasmy and CLL. In response, we have added the description

Results
“Further, we analyzed a random subset of the All of Us Research Program (AoU, n = 40,930)
to confirm our findings in an independent cohort. Heteroplasmy was present in 11,064
(27.0%) individuals with a distribution of heteroplasmy count and mMSS similar to that
observed in the UKB (Supplementary Figure 2A). More specifically, Complex I and D-loop
were the most frequently mutated complex/region. Additionally, mMSS was the lowest in

“We observed similar associations between heteroplasmy and CLL in an independent
cohort, the AoU, using a case-cohort design. In addition to the random subset of 20% of

leading to a total of 87 CLL cases in the case-cohort, with a median follow up of 3.9 (1.6–

Given that mMLC is a relatively newly developed score, it has not been applied to CLL
cohorts. Thus, we would need to reanalyze previously published CLL cohorts with whole
genome sequencing data available. Even though this is part of our roadmap moving
forward, it is not feasible at the current time due to funding and time constraints.

excluded by a lymphocyte filter <5,000/µL) in the UK Biobank. If this is the case, what
is the impact of this on the authors analysis and conclusions?
We agree with the reviewer that information on MBL would add value to this study.
However, given the absence of flow cytometry data, we were not able to identify cases of
MBL. This limitation is stated in the Discussion section:
“Finally, because we did not have flow cytometry data to diagnose prevalent CLL, we had
to rely on lymphocytosis to eliminate potentially undiagnosed CLL, thus likely excluding
some individuals with polyclonal secondary lymphocytosis. On the other hand, we likely
included some individuals with prevalent MBL.”
Considering the clonal nature of MBL, heteroplasmy and L-CHIP, it is possible that MBL
would be associated with both heteroplasmy and L-CHIP, especially in cases that
developed CLL. Nonetheless, the presence of high-risk L-CHIP gene mutations, the
number of L-CHIP mutations and predicted deleterious effect of heteroplasmy are likely to
offer more information on CLL risk, compared to MBL alone. Thus, even if all individuals
with L-CHIP would also present MBL, we expect that genetic information would further
help to define individuals at a higher risk of developing CLL.

We restricted the cohort to only individuals who developed CLL. For the association
between L-CHIP, heteroplasmy, mMSS and time between sampling to diagnosis of CLL, we
used multivariable linear regression models. The analyses were adjusted for age modeled
as a restricted cubic spline (with 4 degrees of freedom), sex, tobacco smoking status
(never or ever), and a history of cancer.
We did see an association between L-CHIP and a shorter time to CLL diagnosis (P = 0.02)
but did not see an association between any heteroplasmy and the time to CLL diagnosis (P
= 0.37).
When assessing the correlation between mMSS and time to CLL diagnosis we found that
individuals with higher mMSS were more likely to have a shorter time to CLL diagnosis
among all individuals who developed CLL (P < 0.01) and restricted to individuals with
heteroplasmy (P = 0.01). Conversely, when individuals with high mMSS (>2) were excluded,
the association was no longer significant (P = 0.26).
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
This work neatly demonstrates that deleterious mitochondrial heteroplasmy can be
used as a novel predictor of chronic lymphocytic leukemia, independent of L-CHIP.
This highlights a promising new biomarker associated with CLL, however while I found
the associative results to be compelling, I have concerns about the causal claims
made throughout the manuscript.
We agree with the reviewer that causality cannot be inferred solely from association data.
Accordingly, our statements regarding potential biological consequences of heteroplasmy
were intentionally non-definitive and we have revised the manuscript to clarify this point.
Also, please see our repones to Reviewer’s 1 point #3 and Reviewer 2.
The authors model for heteroplasmy count and mMSS together, but these variables
are inherently correlated due to mMSS being a cumulative sum over heteroplasmies.
This dependence makes interpreting the functional importance of mMSS difficult. It
may be better to use an average mMLC to separate the functional severity of the
mutations from the total burden. The authors might also consider modelling the risk of
CLL against average mMLC when restricted to only individuals carrying heteroplasmy
(both with and without L-CHIP) to better evaluate the functional importance of
heteroplasmy beyond a marker of clonal expansion.
We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful suggestion. While we recognize the rationale
behind using an average mMLC score (mMSA) to disentangle the functional severity of
mutations from total heteroplasmy burden, we note that this approach may not be
superior to our currently used model. As an example, mMSA would assign the same score
to an individual with two heteroplasmies (both with an mMLC of 0.5) as to someone with
one heteroplasmy of the same mMLC.
That said, in response to the reviewer’s comment, for individuals with heteroplasmy, we
defined the mMSA as mMSS/heteroplasmy count. For individuals without heteroplasmy,
the score was set to 0. We then performed survival analysis using a multivariable Cox-
proportional hazards model for risk of CLL adjusting for age (modeled as a restricted cubic
spline with 4 degrees of freedom), sex, tobacco smoking status (never or ever), and a
history of cancer. The results of this analysis, including heteroplasmy count, mMSS and
mMSA are presented in the table below. We observe that, in the whole cohort and in
analyses restricted to L-CHIP negative individuals, the Z-score for mMSA is lower than that
of mMSS, showing that mMSS better captures the risk for CLL compared to mMSA.
Additionally, please note that, in the manuscript, we evaluated mMSS with and without
adjusting for heteroplasmy count.
Thus, we believe that using mMSS offers more information on CLL risk compared to mMSA.
A further consideration is that mMSS does not account for the VAFs of the contributing
mutations. Variants can often have heteroplasmy dependent effects, and so a VAF
weighted mMSS (or VAF weighted average mMLC) may do better at capturing the
functional burden of these mutations.
We agree with the reviewer that incorporating heteroplasmy VAF could, in theory, provide
additional insight into the functional consequences of mitochondrial mutation both at the
individual cell level and the clone level. We initially considered including VAF as a variable
for our predictive models. However, the interpretation of VAF-based metrics was
confounded by the inherent complexity of mtDNA mutational burden assessment in bulk
DNA samples. The significant variability in mtDNA copy number per cell, the proportion of
mutant mtDNA per cell and the size of hematopoietic clone affected make the
interpretation of the impact of VAF practically infeasible in this context.
In response to reviewer’s suggestion, we have assessed the association between the
maximum heteroplasmy VAF per sample and CLL incidence. No significant association
was observed in all individuals with heteroplasmy (HR = 1.0; 95% CI 0.5–1.7; P = 0.89),
individuals with only one heteroplasmy (HR = 0.8; 95% CI 0.4–1.6; P = 0.46) and in
individuals with a single heteroplasmy with VAF < 50% (HR = 0.7; 95% CI 0.1–3.6; P = 0.70).
We have also assessed the correlation between L-CHIP VAF and heteroplasmy VAF in
individuals harboring one L-CHIP mutation and a single heteroplasmy with a VAF < 50%.
Using both a multivariable linear model (Beta-estimate = 0.0005214; P = 0.12) and a
Spearman’s rank correlation (rho = 0.03; P = 0.16) and found no evidence of significant
correlation.
Together, these findings suggest that heteroplasmy VAF, as derived from bulk sequencing
data, offers limited additional prognostic value and provides little insight into the
functional effect of these mutations.
